messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: output format for bin/print?
parts:
I'm finding a couple things in the output of bin/print confusing.
Here's an example:

------------------------------------------
~/stan(feature/stan-language-paper)$ bin/print --precision=2 samples*.csv
Inference for Stan model: bernoulli_model
4 chains: each with iter=(1000,1000,1000,1000); warmup=(0,0,0,0); thin=(1,1,1,1); 4000 iterations saved.

Warmup took (0.092863, 0.09911, 0.10535, 0.095827) seconds, 0.39315 seconds total
Sampling took (0.089032, 0.088401, 0.097865, 0.087141) seconds, 0.362439 seconds total

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff n_eff/time Rhat
lp__ -7.30e+00 0.02 0.77 -9.45e+00 -7.49e+00 -7.02e+00 -6.80e+00 -6.75e+00 9.76e+02 2.69e+03 1.00e+00
accept_stat__ 5.01e-01 0.05 0.40 2.22e-07 7.52e-02 4.75e-01 9.99e-01 1.00e+00 5.50e+01 1.52e+02 1.03e+00
stepsize__ 2.15e+00 0.13 0.19 1.97e+00 1.97e+00 2.14e+00 2.46e+00 2.46e+00 2.00e+00 5.52e+00 5.69e+13
treedepth__ 4.60e-02 0.00 0.21 0.00e+00 0.00e+00 0.00e+00 0.00e+00 1.00e+00 2.97e+03 8.19e+03 1.00e+00
theta 2.53e-01 0.00 0.12 5.94e-02 1.59e-01 2.35e-01 3.32e-01 5.42e-01 1.76e+03 4.84e+03 1.00e+00

Samples were drawn using NUTS with a diagonal Euclidean metric.
For each parameter, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size,
and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at
convergence, Rhat=1).
------------------------------------------------

I like the warmup and sampling times and the more
explicit indication of the chains. I also like that it's
now dumping the accept stat, stepsize and tree depth.

What is the accept stat?

I still find "thin" a confusing name. I think "keep" is more in line
with the behavior, because thin=1 keeps every sample. If thin=2,
you keep every other sample, and if thin=3, you keep every third sample.

I believe the warmup=(0,0,0,0) indicates that the samples.csv didn't have
warmup "samples"? I'm worried people are going to run Stan then find
this confusing if our default isn't to save and mark warmup "samples".

The timing should be printed with the same precision as everything else.

Shouldn't "precision=2" lead to 2 digits rather than 3 digits of precision?

Is the stepsize sd just because there are four chains?

Can we change n_eff/time to n_eff/s? That does seem to be the unit.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] output format for bin/print?
parts: > What is the accept stat?
Metropolis acceptance probability.

> I still find "thin" a confusing name. I think "keep" is more in line
> with the behavior, because thin=1 keeps every sample. If thin=2,
> you keep every other sample, and if thin=3, you keep every third sample.
Thin is the notation used in BDA -- it's an easy fix on the Stan side is we decide to change it. I have no strong opinions.

> I believe the warmup=(0,0,0,0) indicates that the samples.csv didn't have
> warmup "samples"? I'm worried people are going to run Stan then find
> this confusing if our default isn't to save and mark warmup "samples".

Right, the numbers refer to what was saved. We can add a note making it more explicit, but I think it's safer to default to not saving, as otherwise people might use the warmup samples as regular samples and really mess up their inferences.
> The timing should be printed with the same precision as everything else.
I can fix that. Can you create an issue with the various changes you'd like and assign me?
> Shouldn't "precision=2" lead to 2 digits rather than 3 digits of precision?

Well, yes, but there is a subtly. Here you have numbers like 0.12 -- since there's nothing to the left of the decimal you have two digits of precision to the right. But if everything in the column is shown with the same width, then other numbers will have to go from 4.2 to 4.21.
> Is the stepsize sd just because there are four chains?
Yup.
> Can we change n_eff/time to n_eff/s? That does seem to be the unit.
Sure. I originally wanted "neff/time (samples/s)" but that was way too verbose.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] output format for bin/print?
parts:
On 6/26/13 3:33 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> What is the accept stat?
>
> Metropolis acceptance probability.

For what? NUTS doesn't just generate a proposal then Metropolis
accept/reject.

>> I still find "thin" a confusing name. I think "keep" is more in line
>> with the behavior, because thin=1 keeps every sample. If thin=2,
>> you keep every other sample, and if thin=3, you keep every third sample.
>
> Thin is the notation used in BDA -- it's an easy fix on the Stan side is we decide to change it. I have no strong opinions.

I know. It's also used in the other packages.

I just thought that this would be the time to change it.
In the same spirit as changing "burnin" to "warmup",
we could change "thin" to "keep" or something similar.

>> I believe the warmup=(0,0,0,0) indicates that the samples.csv didn't have
>> warmup "samples"? I'm worried people are going to run Stan then find
>> this confusing if our default isn't to save and mark warmup "samples".
>
> Right, the numbers refer to what was saved. We can add a note making it more explicit, but I think it's safer to default to not saving, as otherwise people might use the warmup samples as regular samples and really mess up their inferences.

I think that makes sense from the command-line. It's a little
different in R because of the way things like traceplots are generated
and how the accessors are implemented to let you ignore the
warmup iterations.

>> The timing should be printed with the same precision as everything else.
>
> I can fix that. Can you create an issue with the various changes you'd like and assign me?

That's the only definite one at the moment.

There's also the issue of printing every iteration.

>> Shouldn't "precision=2" lead to 2 digits rather than 3 digits of precision?
>
> Well, yes, but there is a subtly. Here you have numbers like 0.12 -- since there's nothing to the left of the decimal you have two digits of precision to the right. But if everything in the column is shown with the same width, then other numbers will have to go from 4.2 to 4.21.

I agree that it's not a very well defined problem.

Here's what R does, which I also don't understand:

> print(1.23,digits=2)
[1] 1.2

> print(c(0.981,1.23),digits=2)
[1] 0.98 1.23

> print(c(0.00001,1.234567),digits=2)
[1] 0.00001 1.23457

My main concerns are that the scientific notation is
hard to read and that the command-line and R should
be doing something similar. (Though as I just said, I'm
not even sure what R's doing!)

The more I think about it, the more I like the scientific
notation's ability to keep everything lined up with the
same number of digits.

The real problem is that the columns aren't coherent in what
we're printing --- they can be on all different scales from
the log probability (huge negative) down to small hierarchical
variances.

>> Is the stepsize sd just because there are four chains?
>
> Yup.
>
>> Can we change n_eff/time to n_eff/s? That does seem to be the unit.
>
> Sure. I originally wanted "neff/time (samples/s)" but that was way too verbose.

Thanks. I created an issue.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] output format for bin/print?
parts:
>> Metropolis acceptance probability.
>
> For what? NUTS doesn't just generate a proposal then Metropolis
> accept/reject.
Right. It's the average acceptance probability of all points in the NUTS slice.

> I know. It's also used in the other packages.
>
> I just thought that this would be the time to change it.
> In the same spirit as changing "burnin" to "warmup",
> we could change "thin" to "keep" or something similar.
If Stan becomes ubiquitous we really could change a ton of vocabulary. Such power, such responsibility. :-)

> I agree that it's not a very well defined problem.
>
> Here's what R does, which I also don't understand:
>
> > print(1.23,digits=2)
> [1] 1.2
>
> > print(c(0.981,1.23),digits=2)
> [1] 0.98 1.23
>
> > print(c(0.00001,1.234567),digits=2)
> [1] 0.00001 1.23457
>
> My main concerns are that the scientific notation is
> hard to read and that the command-line and R should
> be doing something similar. (Though as I just said, I'm
> not even sure what R's doing!)
>
> The more I think about it, the more I like the scientific
> notation's ability to keep everything lined up with the
> same number of digits.
>
> The real problem is that the columns aren't coherent in what
> we're printing --- they can be on all different scales from
> the log probability (huge negative) down to small hierarchical
> variances.

Definitely, and because of that I don't think we can get away from scientific notation.

Here's what we do right now. The precision sets the number of digits to show, and for each column we scan through the values to see the number of digits that would have to be printed to achieve that precision (a precision of 2 for 0.000012 six additional characters, for example) to determine the max number of printed digits. If that's too large we switch to scientific notation, otherwise we print in fixed.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] output format for bin/print?
parts:
OK, that one was modified by me to make it fit.
Here's the real output:
mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff n_eff/time Rhat
> We define precision to be the number of digits past the decimal place.

In scientific notation, you're getting two such decimals. For
example 2.5e-01 is 0.25, but you only get one decimal place in
sd and then one decimal for only half the entries in se_mean.
Here's precision=3:
mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff

parts:
I know this is all nitpicking, but it's important for
usability.

Would anybody mind dropping one of the intervals, either the
95% or the 50%? I don't care if the interval we go with is
an 80% interval or whatever, but I don't think we need two
intervals. (I'd stick with 95% or 90% and drop the 50%
interval.)

I like n_eff/time, but that'd probably be the next logical
thing to drop.

Also, changing se_mean to se, and n_eff/time to n_eff/s would
save several more chars in the width.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] output format for bin/print?
parts: Precision is number of digits past the decimal place in the selected format. So, yes, there is more information displayed in scientific notation but (a) it would look awkward if the mantissas didn't match and (b) there would be inconsistent formatting if a column had a number much larger than 1 and one less than one (for example 111 and 0.1.
